tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

content.text:
Yes, Claude Code makes `.claude/` itself. It's the program doing it, not me: I never write there. Your stat times fit a directory made at launch. I can add two things from looking at io_uring-2-zcr-v4-x1 just now:

- Its `.claude/` holds only `.cc-writes/`, which is empty and mode 700. My earlier timing tests suggest it's a temp area for writing settings files: write a temp file, then rename it into place.
- Its `.gitignore` doesn't list `/.claude` at all, and its repo is still clean. jj and git don't track empty directories, so an unignored `.claude/` shows nothing until a real file appears in it.

The later 15:13 mtime on `.claude` most likely comes from the sandbox making and removing its placeholder files there on each command. We think that's the cause, but I haven't checked it.

**Nested vs external doesn't matter here.** `~/.claude/projects/<mangled>` is per-user: transcripts, and the memory directory you don't use. The project's own `.claude/` is per-checkout: settings, agents, commands, skills. Claude Code makes the second one wherever the agent-repo lives. Naming the agent dir `.claude` was the one setup where the two shared a directory, so its contents rode along in the agent-repo by accident.

**I'd recommend against going back to `.claude` as the agent dir:**
- `settings.local.json` is machine-local by design: sandbox on here, off there. Committed to the agent-repo, it would follow you from the 3900x to the 7600x and flip settings on each pull.
- The sandbox protects paths under `.claude/` and puts its placeholder files there. That's a poor place for a jj repo the agent has to write to.
- "Committed in the agent-repo" isn't the visibility you're after either. Nobody reads that repo's diffs.

**I'd also recommend against committing `.claude/` to the work-repo,** for the same machine-local reason.

**What I'd do: narrow the work-repo's ignore and add an alarm.**
- Replace `/.claude` with `/.claude/settings.local.json` and `/.claude/.cc-writes/`. This follows your own reasoning from the last cycle. If anyone makes a shareable `.claude/settings.json`, `agents/` or `commands/`, it shows up in `jj st` and gets decided on instead of hiding.
- Have vc-x1 warn when `.claude/settings.local.json` exists, at acquaint or in `validate`. That gives you the "public, not hidden" part you want: the file can't be committed by accident, and it can't go unnoticed either. Right now this project has one, the sandbox-off file pinned by the read-only `.claude`, and the warning would point at it.

Both would be a Todo entry or a cycle, on your go. The init default (whether it writes the narrow lines or none) belongs in the same entry.

The plain version: Claude Code always makes a `.claude/` folder in the project, wherever the agent-repo lives. Its one real file, `settings.local.json`, belongs to one machine, so it shouldn't be committed anywhere. Ignore just that file and the temp folder, have vc-x1 warn when the file exists, and anything else that appears in `.claude/` stays visible.

content.text:
You're right. I tested two paths and generalized from them. The accurate claim: the two paths we tested make those two entries. Other Claude Code features may write elsewhere in `.claude/`, and we haven't looked.

**My answer for an agent dir other than `.claude`:**

```
/.claude/settings.local.json
/.claude/.cc-writes/
```

What iiac-perf shows makes the case better than vc-x1 does. Its two files are two different kinds of thing:

- **`settings.json` is hand-written and shareable.** "Common commands I use that shouldn't need approval" is meant to travel with the repo. In the work-repo, it's public and reviewed, which is your stated goal. If the rule stays "no settings in `.claude`", the narrow ignore still makes it show up in `jj st` the moment one appears, so the rule can be enforced.
- **`settings.local.json` is where "don't ask again" approvals pile up.** Look at what's in iiac-perf's: one-off sed commands, session scratchpad paths, `/home/nps-gnc/...`, ssh invocations to the 7600x, your email in a curl header, and the sandbox-off toggle. It belongs to one machine and one history, and it shouldn't be committed anywhere.
- **`.cc-writes/` is cheap insurance.** It's empty at rest, but we think it stages temp files. jj snapshots on every command, so it could catch one mid-write.

**What the narrow form gives up:** if some untested feature writes a machine-local file elsewhere in `.claude/`, jj auto-tracks it and it shows up in the review diff. With `/.claude`, it would hide. That's the same trade you chose for the sandbox names: an unknown file surfaces rather than hides. And for a work-repo, the diff review is where it gets caught.

**A finding in iiac-perf, which I've only looked at, not changed:** its agent dir is `.claude`, and `git ls-files` in that agent-repo lists both `settings.json` and `settings.local.json`. So the local file, with the contents above, is committed and pushed wherever that agent-repo's remote is. iiac-perf has its own agent, so by our rules that's a message to it, not a change I'd make. Say if you want one sent.

The plain version: when the agent-repo isn't `.claude`, ignore only the machine-local settings file and the temp folder, and let anything else in `.claude/` show up for review. iiac-perf shows why: its local file is full of one-machine approvals, and because its agent-repo is `.claude`, that file is currently committed and pushed.

content.text:
Not by definition. iiac-perf's copy looks hand-edited, but Claude Code can write that file too.

**iiac-perf's copy looks hand-edited.** In its agent-repo history, it was created on 2026-07-04 and got two small additions the next day. Three things point to a hand edit, by you or by an agent using an edit tool:

- **A `_comment` key.** Settings don't have one. It's a human's note.
- **The blank line after `_comment`.** It's there in the first commit and still there after both additions. A program that loads and re-serializes JSON would normally drop it.
- **The rule style.** It uses broad wildcards like `Bash(cargo *)`. The local file instead has the exact commands that were approved one by one, such as `Bash(cargo build:*)` and the long one-off sed lines.

**What Claude Code writes, by our tests and my belief:**
- **Tested:** `/sandbox` writes `settings.local.json`.
- **We think, untested:** a "don't ask again" answer to a permission prompt adds to `settings.local.json`. That fits how the local file reads.
- **We think, untested:** `/permissions` can add a rule to either file, because it asks whether a rule is project-shared (`settings.json`) or local. So a `settings.json` can also be made by the tool.

So the split isn't "handmade vs generated". The split is "meant to be shared" vs "this machine only". That's what makes the narrow ignore right. `settings.json` is the one Claude Code treats as shareable, so it should be visible. `settings.local.json` is the one it treats as per-machine, so it should be ignored.

The plain version: iiac-perf's `settings.json` was almost certainly written by hand, judging by its comment and formatting. Claude Code can probably also write to that file. What matters is that `settings.json` is the shared file and `settings.local.json` is the per-machine one, and the ignore lines follow that split.

content.text:
Yes, that works, and it covers every layout.

| Agent dir | Where `settings.local.json` lands | Line that ignores it |
|---|---|---|
| `.claude` (nested) | agent-repo root | agent-repo: `/settings.local.json` |
| `.agent-session` or any other nested name | `work/.claude/` | work-repo: `/.claude/settings.local.json` |
| external (`../x.agent`) | `work/.claude/` | work-repo: `/.claude/settings.local.json` |

In each layout, the line that doesn't apply ignores a file that never shows up there, so it costs nothing. When the agent dir is `.claude`, the work-repo needs `/.claude` regardless, and the narrow line is redundant but harmless. `vc-x1 init` can write both lines every time without checking the layout.

Three details:

- **Anchor the agent-repo pattern** as `/settings.local.json`. Unanchored, it would match that name anywhere in the agent-repo.
- **Should `.cc-writes/` get the same treatment?** Its line pair would be `/.claude/.cc-writes/` in the work-repo and `/.cc-writes/` in the agent-repo. It's empty at rest, so it's insurance only. Leaving it out is defensible.
- **An ignore line doesn't untrack a file.** Where the file is already committed, as in iiac-perf's agent-repo, it also needs `jj file untrack settings.local.json`, and the copies already pushed stay in history. That's for iiac-perf's agent, and could go in the same message.

For vc-x1, this would be one cycle:

- the `init` default
- vc-x1's own `.gitignore`: `/.claude` becomes `/.claude/settings.local.json`
- vc-x1's agent-repo `.gitignore` gets `/settings.local.json`
- the notes findings

The warning-when-present idea can come later. Say the word to file the cycle as a Todo entry.

The plain version: yes. Ignore `.claude/settings.local.json` in the work-repo and `settings.local.json` in the agent-repo, and the machine-local file stays uncommitted whatever the agent dir is called or wherever it lives. A repo that already committed the file also has to untrack it, since an ignore line doesn't remove a tracked file.

26	  - Place when unblocked: first.
27	- **Sync's remote look stops spawning git.** (wink + agent, 2026-10-09) Sync learns where a
28	  remote's bookmarks are by spawning `git ls-remote`, and downloads the commits of the ones that
29	  moved by spawning a `git fetch` that moves no ref, the sixth entry of the spawn register in
30	  `clippy.toml` and the one spawn of `git`. Replace `git_command` and its two callers in
31	  `src/jj/session.rs` with jj-lib's query, delete the `#[allow]`, and close the entry.

33	    `rg -i 'ls.remote' src/` in the jj-lib source prints nothing, and its git subprocess layer is
34	    `pub(crate)`. An upstream feature request, once filed or found, is named here.
35	  - Place when unblocked: first, being one function.

39	Entries are in priority order, the first highest, and reprioritizing is moving an entry. Each is a

41	[todo-backlog.md](notes/todo-backlog.md). Use the [Prose form](agent-data/prose.md#prose-form).

45

47	says the session's background commands end when the session does, and so the lock is never
48	stale. What it does not say: a holder ended that way skips the sandbox's cleanup, and leaves an

52

54	
55	(wink + agent, 2026-10-11) A later stage of a cycle, its closing most often, adds to the work
56	commit already pushed, and `vc-x1 push` can only make a new commit on each side. So the one
57	work-repo commit needs to reference several agent-repo commits. Today that is done by hand:
58	a `jj squash`, a `jj describe` with a trailer written by hand, and then the push.

64:## Todo format
65-
66-`TODO.md` has these sections, in this order. Each item in them is a short description with
67-reference links to more detail.
68-
69-- `## Continuation notes`: where the agent was, for the agent that comes next. Ephemeral, never a
70-  record, `_None._` by default, written before a restart or a loss of context, and reset by the
71-  agent that reads it, after filing each fact into its home or keeping the bullet whose fact has
72-  none, so a reset never destroys the only copy of anything.
73-- `## In Progress`: the running cycle's record ([Cycle-record](../AGENTS.md#cycle-record)).
74-- `## Waiting`: important work that cannot start yet. Each entry names what it waits on and its
75-  rank once unblocked, and every opening checks the conditions.
76-- `## Todo`: entries in priority order, the first highest. The long-tail backlog is in
77-  [todo-backlog.md](../notes/todo-backlog.md).
78-- `## Ideas`: unranked.
79-- `## Bugs`: a pointer to [bugs.md](../notes/bugs.md).
80-- `## Closed`: the last cycle's finished record.
81-- `# References`: the file-local reference definitions, the file's last section ([Reference
82-  numbering](#reference-numbering)).
83-
84-Every adopter has one `TODO.md` of this shape. It is not an agent-file, since its content is the
85-project's record, and the payload ships it as a skeleton: `## In Progress` reading
86-`_No cycle currently in progress._`, the other sections empty.
87-
88-An entry is a `###` heading, its title, followed by its text. Priority is file order, the first
89-entry the highest, and reprioritizing is moving the entry. The title is unique within its file and
90-is the entry's anchor, so a citation is a link, `[title](TODO.md#<slug>)`, that the anchor check
91-verifies ([Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) for the text). Entries carry no number: a rank number
92-renumbers on every move and every citation that holds one goes stale, which is why the numbered
93-form was retired (2026-08-27). An entry's sub-entries, when it groups several, are bullets with a
94-bold title, cited by the bold text.

### Every repo ignores Claude Code's settings.local.json

(wink + agent, 2026-10-14) Claude Code writes `.claude/settings.local.json` in the project
directory, the per-machine file: `/sandbox` writes it there on its first toggle, and we think a
permission prompt's "don't ask again" adds to it. Its content belongs to one machine and one
history, the sandbox's on or off among it, so it is never committed. iiac-perf's agent-repo is
`.claude`, and there the file is tracked and pushed. The shared `settings.json` beside it stays
visible. One line in each repo covers every layout, nested, external, or single:

- Work-repo, and a single-repo workspace: `/.claude/settings.local.json`. `init` writes neither
  today (`render_work_gitignore` and `GITIGNORE_APP_ONLY` in `src/init.rs`), and vc-x1's own
  `.gitignore` drops its whole-directory `/.claude` for it, so anything else Claude Code writes
  there shows in `jj st` and is reviewed.
- Agent-repo: `/settings.local.json`, which matters only when the agent dir is `.claude`, and
  harms nothing otherwise. `init` writes it into `GITIGNORE_SESSION`, and vc-x1's
  `.agent-session/.gitignore` takes it.
- Decide at the opening: whether `.cc-writes/`, the empty mode-700 directory the sandbox's first
  command makes beside it, gets the same pair (`/.claude/.cc-writes/`, `/.cc-writes/`).
- Record the findings in [session-lock.md](notes/session-lock.md#the-sandboxs-placeholder-files):
  `.claude/` is made on demand, not at launch, `.cc-writes/` by the sandbox's first Bash
  command and `settings.local.json` by `/sandbox`, both tested 2026-10-14 in fresh empty
  directories.
- Later, not this cycle: a warning, at acquaint or in `validate`, when the file exists.

I've added the entry to the top of `## Todo` as **"Every repo ignores Claude Code's settings.local.json"**. `vc-x1 validate --fast` passed. The edit is in the working copy and uncommitted, so it'll go in with the next cycle's commit.

The entry covers:
- **Work-repo and single-repo workspaces:** add `/.claude/settings.local.json`. vc-x1's own `.gitignore` drops its whole-directory `/.claude` for it.
- **Agent-repo:** add `/settings.local.json`. That goes in init's agent-repo default and in vc-x1's `.agent-session/.gitignore`.
- **`.cc-writes/`:** whether it gets the same pair of lines is left to decide at the opening.
- **Findings for the notes:** the two tested facts go into `notes/session-lock.md`. `.claude/` appears on demand, not at launch: `.cc-writes/` from the sandbox's first Bash command, `settings.local.json` from `/sandbox`.
- **Out of scope:** the warning when the file exists comes later. Untracking iiac-perf's copy is a message to iiac-perf's agent.

A correction to what I said before: `init` doesn't currently write any `settings.local.json` line. The work-repo default is `/target /<agent_dir> /.git /.jj`, the single-repo default is the same minus the agent dir, and the agent-repo default is `.git .jj` (all in `src/init.rs`). So `init` changes in all three places, single-repo included, which the entry now says.

I put it first because it's small and practical. Move it if you'd rank it differently.

The plain version: the Todo entry is written and waiting in the working copy. It also corrects something I said earlier: `init` doesn't add any settings line today, so all three of its default ignore files need one.
